blocks.text: — — — — pour out chickpeas generously to the brawling people, so that the old men may remember our sunny Floralia. — — — [II, 587] Thus in the Scetic desert of Egypt, where the monks professed a remarkable frugality, [col. 49] roasted chickpeas served them as food. Cassian, in the place cited above, on Abbot Serenus: He brought in a basket containing roasted chickpeas, which they call trogalia, of which we took only five grains each. Hence Tertullian uses cicercula [chickling] for a thing of very little value, when he writes thus against Marcion, book 1, chapter 11: The God of Marcion ought to have produced at least one chickling, so that he might be proclaimed a new Triptolemus. Among the Greeks too, ἐρεβίνθινος [erebinthinos], that is, cicernus [of chickpea], is taken for worthless. Hesychius: Ἐρεβίνθινος Διόνυσος· οὐδενὸς ἄξιος, παρά τινα παροιμίαν ἐρεβίνθινος ζωμός [Erebinthinos Dionysos; oudenos axios, para tina paroimian erebinthinos zōmos]; Chickpea Bacchus (chickpea wine), that is, of no value; in a certain proverb chickpea broth is so called. Likewise Suidas: Ἐρεβίνθινος Διόνυσος· ἐπὶ τῶν μηδενὸς ἀξίων [Erebinthinos Dionysos; epi tōn mēdenos axiōn]. Chickpea Bacchus, of things of no value. Plutarch, in the Rom. Quaest., chapter 95, observes that τὸν λάθυρον, καὶ τὸν ἐρέβινθον [ton lathyron, kai ton erebinthon], the chickling and the chickpea, were forbidden and detested foods for some, but for a jocular reason: namely ὡς παρωνύμους τοῦ Ἐρέβους, καὶ τῆς Λήθης [hōs parōnymous tou Erebous, kai tēs Lēthēs], as alluding to Erebus and Lethe (the river of the underworld). For as ἐρέβινθος [erebinthos] alludes to Erebus, so λάθυρος [lathyros] to Lethe. He adds that pulses were very much used πρὸς τὰ περίδειπνα, καὶ τὰς προκλήσεις τῶν νεκρῶν [pros ta perideipna, kai tas prosklēseis tōn nekrōn], at funeral meals and for the summoning of the dead. But this pertains rather to the bean or the lentil. For on the bean Pliny, book 18, ch. 12: The Pythagorean opinion (on the bean) condemned it, as others have reported, because the souls of the dead are in it. For this reason it is certainly used in rites for deceased parents. Varro also reports that for these reasons the Flamen does not eat it, since mournful letters are also found on its flower. And Festus: It is not permitted to the Flamen Dialis either to touch or to name the bean, because it is thought to pertain to the dead. For it is thrown to the ghosts at the Lemuria, and used in sacrifices to deceased parents, and the letters of mourning seem to appear on its flower. Similar is the fact that the ancients counted the lentil among τὰ πένθιμα [ta penthima], mournful things, καὶ προτίθενται τοῖς νέκυσιν [kai protithentai tois nekysin], and set it before the dead, as Plutarch notes in the Crassus and Appian in the Parthica. That the Jews were not entirely free of this superstition is attested by these words of Jerome to Paula on the death of Blaesilla: And to this day the Jews, weeping, with bare feet, rolled in the dust, lie on sackcloth; and, so that nothing may be lacking to superstition, by a most empty rite of the Pharisees they take lentils as their first food, showing, no doubt, for what kind of dish they lost the birthright. But concerning the chickpea I have found only in Pliny that religion uses it at night vigils. If, however, along with the bean and the lentil, the chickpea and the chickling also belonged to funeral meals, as Plutarch seems to hint, then, since the reasons adduced have little to do with the matter, I would believe the ancients had nothing else in view than that a time of mourning befits thin and frugal foods, such as all pulses are, which fill the body but nourish it little. Accordingly the chief of Nebuchadnezzar's eunuchs feared that if Daniel and his companions ate pulses, their faces would look sadder and leaner than those of the other youths whom the king kept in his retinue. See Dan. I, 8. etc. It should be noted [II, 588] that there, in verses 12 and 16, pulses are not called קטניות, as elsewhere by the Hebrews, but זרעים, or זרענים. This word is more general. For זרעים or זרענים are any seeds whatever. Accordingly the Greek version, which is that of Theodotion, has σπέρματα [spermata]. And Maimonides defines what זרעונים, seeds, are in the treatise On Mixed Kinds, book 1, ch. 8: הזרעונים נחלקין לשלושה חלקים האחד מהם הוא הנקרא תבואה והיא חמשה מינין החטים והכוסמין והשעורין ושבולת שועל והשיפון והשני מהן הוא הנקרא קטנית והן כל זרעים הנאכל לאדם חוץ מן התבואה כגון הפול והאפונים והדוחן והאורז והשומשמין והפרגין והספיר וכיוצא בהן והשלישי מהן הוא הנקרא זרעוני גנה והן שאר זרעונין שאינן ראויין למאכל אדם והפרי [col. 50] של אותר הזרע מאכל אדם כגון זרע הבצלין והשומין וזרע החציר והקצח וזרע לפת וכיוצא בהן, Seeds are divided into three kinds. The first is of those called produce (grain crops, σιτώδη [sitōdē]). Of these there are five kinds: wheat, spelt, barley, fox's ear (oats, whose ear resembles a fox's tail), rye. The second is of those they call pulses, that is, all seeds eaten by man, such as beans, peas, millet, rice, sesame, poppy, chickling and the like. The third is of those called garden seeds, which are themselves not fit for eating, but what grows from them is eaten by man, such as onions, garlic, leeks, nigella, turnips and the like. Yet in Daniel זרעי is explained as ὄσπρια [ospria], pulses, by Josephus and the Greek Scholiast, Tertullian, Jerome, R. Selomo, Saadias Gaon, Aben Ezra, Joseph son of Jachia, etc. And they could just as well be called זרעים, that is, seeds, in Hebrew as ὄσπρια [ospria] in Greek. For they are called ὄσπρια [ospria] for σπόρια [sporia], ἀπὸ τῆς σπορᾶς [apo tēs sporas], from sowing. So this Greek name corresponds exactly to the Hebrew. But in Greek they are also called χεδροπὰ [chedropa], as if χειρόδροπα [cheirodropa], just as in Latin legumina [pulses], because they are gathered (leguntur) by hand. Referring to this, Nicander, Theriaca, verse 752, says.
